finding.claim: /settings/email is protected only by @login_optional, so anonymous requests reach set_email with uid=None and no abort occurs.
finding.source: Anonymous HTTP POST to /settings/email with no uid in the session (routes.py:22 sets g.uid=None).
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, 'new@example.org') at routes.py:37 (account email change; stub at routes.py:48-49).

trace.note: g.uid = session.get('uid') -> None for anonymous client; no abort
set_email stub; real implementation would receive uid=None

finding.guards_checked: login_optional (routes.py:19-25) never rejects; handler has no session check; no CSRF check visible in this file; request body not used.

verdict.guard_found: none. login_optional (routes.py:19-25) only sets g.uid = session.get("uid") (line 22) and never aborts. change_email (routes.py:35-38) has no session check and calls set_email(g.uid, "new@example.org") unconditionally at line 37. Contrast login_required (routes.py:8-16), which does abort(401) and is applied to change_password (routes.py:42) but not to change_email.
verdict.reason: An anonymous POST to /settings/email reaches set_email(None, "new@example.org") at routes.py:37 because login_optional (routes.py:22) never rejects, so the route has no authentication; the impact is limited by the set_email stub at routes.py:48-49 being a no-op in this file, so the real effect depends on the production implementation.

finding.claim: /settings/password sets the account password to the hardcoded literal 'hunter2' without reading client input or verifying the current password.
finding.source: Any holder of a valid session POSTing to /settings/password.
finding.sink: set_password(g.uid, 'hunter2') at routes.py:44 (password change; stub at routes.py:52-53).

trace.note: 'uid' not in session -> abort(401); authentication enforced

finding.guards_checked: login_required enforces authentication only. No input read, no current-password re-authentication, no password strength check. Violates org policy against hardcoded credentials.

verdict.guard_found: login_required (routes.py:8-16) enforces only that 'uid' is in the session (abort(401) at line 12) and sets g.uid. Nothing checks a current password, reads input, or otherwise limits what change_password does. The hardcoded 'hunter2' literal is passed unconditionally at line 44.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the file: @login_required is at routes.py:42, the session check and abort(401) are at 11-12, g.uid is set at 13, and set_password(g.uid, "hunter2") is at 44, so any holder of a valid session can set the account password to a known constant with no re-authentication (routes.py:44). The impact depends on the real set_password, since the stub at lines 52-53 does nothing.

finding.claim: State-changing POST routes /settings/email and /settings/password have no visible CSRF protection, so a cross-site request can act on a logged-in victim's session if SameSite cookies are not enforced.
finding.source: Cross-site page causing a logged-in victim's browser to send a POST to the app.
finding.sink: set_email at routes.py:37 and set_password at routes.py:44.

trace.note: session cookie is the only authenticator for login_required routes
session cookie also sets g.uid for login_optional route

The only relevant control is the session check in login_required (routes.py:11-12), which gates /settings/password but not /settings/email, which uses login_optional (routes.py:35, 22). Browser or app SameSite enforcement is not visible in the code.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code (routes.py:34, 41, 11, 22), and no CSRF guard exists in this file (routes.py:34-45), but whether a cross-site POST carries the session cookie depends on SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE and browser defaults, which are not in the code available, so the finding cannot be confirmed or refuted from it.
